2027-06-13.title: Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar … and become a noble cedar
Lord, it is good to give thanks to you
We walk by faith, not by sight
It is like a mustard seed, the smallest of all the seeds on earth
2027-06-13.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The Sundays after Pentecost and Corpus Christi resume the green Sundays of Ordinary Time. St Antony of Padua (13 June) falls on the Sunday this year and is not celebrated at Mass, though popular devotions to him may still be held outside Mass. The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary 92:2–3, 13–14, 15–16 = NRSV 92:1–2, 12–13, 14–15). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-13.verse: The kingdom of God is as if someone would scatter seed on the ground, and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.
theo: The green Sundays have returned. After the great feasts of Easter, Pentecost, the Trinity and Corpus Christi, the Church puts on the colour of growing things, and today's readings are almost all about growth: a sprig of cedar, a palm tree, seed scattered on the ground, a mustard bush full of birds. The first reading comes from Ezekiel, a priest who was taken to Babylon with the first exiles in 597 before Christ. In chapter 17 he tells a riddle about two great eagles and a cedar of Lebanon: the kings of the nations break off the top of Israel's royal tree and carry it away. The house of David looks finished. Then God himself speaks: “Thus says the Lord God: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar; I will set it out. I will break off a tender one from the topmost of its young twigs; I myself will plant it on a high and lofty mountain.” Notice the word “I myself,” repeated. What the great powers could only break, God alone can plant. And the tender sprig will become something no one expected: “On the mountain height of Israel I will plant it, in order that it may produce boughs and bear fruit, and become a noble cedar. Under it every kind of bird will live; in the shade of its branches will nest winged creatures of every kind.” Then comes the law of God's way of working: “I bring low the high tree, I make high the low tree; I dry up the green tree and make the dry tree flourish. I the Lord have spoken; I will accomplish it.” The Church has always heard in this tender shoot a promise of the Messiah from David's line, and in the birds of every kind the nations who will find shelter in his kingdom.

The Psalm takes up the same picture and gives it to every faithful person: “The righteous flourish like the palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the Lord; they flourish in the courts of our God. In old age they still produce fruit; they are always green and full of sap.” Here is a beautiful promise for the elderly in our parishes: age is not the end of fruitfulness. The grandmother who prays the rosary for her scattered children, the old man who still comes to the first Mass every morning, are “always green.” And the Psalm begins where all growth must begin, with thanksgiving: “It is good to give thanks to the Lord, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night.”

St Paul, in the Second Letter to the Corinthians, speaks of a growth we cannot see: the hidden ripening of our lives towards God. “So we are always confident; even though we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.” Paul does not despise this life in the body, but he knows it is not the whole story: “we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.” So whatever happens, near or far, “we make it our aim to please him.” And then a sober line: “For all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive recompense for what has been done in the body, whether good or evil.” A seed is judged by its harvest. What we sow in the body, in our families, our work and our prayer, will one day be gathered in.

In the Gospel Jesus tells two short parables, found together only in Mark. The first is the seed that grows by itself: a farmer scatters seed, “and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how. The earth produces of itself, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head.” The farmer does his part: he sows, and at harvest he goes in “with his sickle.” But the growing is not his work. Every farmer in Kerala who has sown paddy with the first monsoon rains knows this patience: you cannot pull the shoots up to make them grow faster. The kingdom of God works like that in a parish, in a family, in a soul: quietly, by night as well as by day, by a power that is not ours. The second parable is the mustard seed, “the smallest of all the seeds on earth,” which grows into “the greatest of all shrubs, and puts forth large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” Jesus is echoing Ezekiel's cedar, but he chooses a humble garden plant instead of a mighty tree. The kingdom begins small: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve fishermen and tax collectors, a few women who followed him, a handful of bread on an altar. Mark adds that Jesus spoke “the word to them, as they were able to hear it,” and explained everything in private to his disciples. God does not force growth; he sows, waits and explains, patiently, as we are able to hear.
conn: The chapter is an allegory. The first “great eagle” is Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who in 597 before Christ took King Jehoiachin, “the top of the cedar,” into exile (17:3–4, 12); the second eagle is Egypt, to which King Zedekiah turned for help. The closing oracle (17:22–24) moves from politics to promise: God himself will replant the royal line.

The great cedars of the Lebanon mountains were the finest timber of the ancient world; Solomon used them for the Temple (1 Kings 5:6). In the prophets the cedar is an image of kings and empires, sometimes proud and cut down (Isaiah 2:13), sometimes, as here, a sign of God's own planting.

In the Old Testament a great tree sheltering birds is a picture of a kingdom that gives shelter to the nations: Ezekiel 31:6 (“All the birds of the air made their nests in its boughs”) and Daniel 4:12 use the same image. When Jesus says the birds nest in the shade of the mustard plant, his hearers would have caught the echo: the nations will find a home in God's kingdom.

The black mustard that grows around the Lake of Galilee has a tiny seed, about one millimetre across, yet in a season the plant can grow taller than a man. In Jewish speech “small as a mustard seed” was a proverb for the very smallest thing.

Mark 4:28 uses the Greek word automatē, from which our word “automatic” comes. It does not mean that the kingdom grows without God; it means that it grows without the farmer's control. The power of growth is in the seed and the soil God has made.

“At once he goes in with his sickle, because the harvest has come” (Mark 4:29) recalls Joel 3:13: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.” In the prophets the harvest is an image of God's final judgment, which Paul also names in today's second reading.

This chapter is Mark's collection of parables: the sower (4:1–20), the lamp (4:21–25), the seed growing secretly (4:26–29, found only in Mark) and the mustard seed (4:30–32). It ends with the storm on the lake (4:35–41), next Sunday's Gospel.

Paul's word in 2 Corinthians 5:10 is bēma, the raised platform from which a magistrate gave judgment. The Corinthians knew one well: in the forum of their own city Paul had stood before the bēma of the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12).

Born in Lisbon about 1195, he became a Franciscan after seeing the bodies of the first Franciscan martyrs brought back from Morocco. A great preacher, he died near Padua on 13 June 1231 and was canonised within a year; Pope Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946.
altar: At the presentation of the gifts the priest says over the bread: “Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation, for through your goodness we have received the bread we offer you: fruit of the earth and work of human hands.” The grain that grew “he does not know how” is laid on the altar. By the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of Christ it becomes truly the Body of Christ, the seed of eternal life planted in us.

The Eucharist is the mustard seed of the kingdom: a small piece of bread, a little wine, and yet the whole Christ, Body, Blood, soul and divinity, under these humble signs. From this small beginning the Church grows, and under its shade the nations find their home.
outline: Hold up a mustard seed, or any small seed, and ask: how much of a tree can you see in this?
Point 1 · I myself will plant it
God replants the broken cedar of David; what the powers break, God alone can plant.
Point 2 · He does not know how
The seed grows by itself, night and day; our part is to sow and wait.
Point 3 · The smallest of all the seeds
The kingdom begins small and gives shelter to all.
Growth we cannot see, and a harvest before the judgment seat of Christ.
A farmer in the monsoon rain, sowing and then going home to sleep, trusting the earth and the sky.
“The seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.”
live: This week say one word of faith, one kind word, or one invitation to prayer, and leave the growth to God.
Name a person you have prayed for a long time without seeing change. Keep praying, and thank God for the growth you cannot see.
Visit or call an elderly person this week: “in old age they still produce fruit.” Ask them to pray for you.
Each night this week ask: what did I sow today in my family, my work and my prayer?
fathers: Christ himself is the mustard seed. He seemed small and despised when he was buried in the earth like a grain; but when he rose he grew into a tree whose branches cover the world, and the souls of the faithful rest in his shade like birds (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke, Book 7).

With the mustard seed the Lord encouraged his disciples. They were few and poor and weak; he showed them that the preaching would spread over the whole earth, and that what began in a few would grow beyond all expectation (Homilies on Matthew, 46).

A man casts seed on the ground when he places a good intention in his heart; he sleeps when he rests in the hope that comes from a good work; he rises night and day as he advances through good times and bad. The seed sprouts and grows while he does not know how, for even when he cannot measure his growth, the virtue once conceived goes on to maturity (Homilies on Ezekiel, Book 2, Homily 3).

Let us sing here in hope, so that we may sing there in possession. Here we walk by faith, there we shall see; sing now as travellers sing, to lighten the toil, and keep walking (Sermon 256, on the Alleluia).
magis: The Word of the Lord is compared to a seed sown in a field; those who hear it with faith and are numbered among the little flock of Christ have received the kingdom itself. Then, by its own power, the seed sprouts and grows until the harvest. The Church is on earth the seed and the beginning of that kingdom.

Jesus' invitation to enter his kingdom comes in the form of parables, a characteristic feature of his teaching. Through them he calls people to the feast of the kingdom, but also asks for a radical choice: words are not enough, deeds are required.

Death puts an end to human life as the time open to accepting or rejecting the grace of God manifested in Christ. Each person receives an eternal retribution in his immortal soul at the very moment of death, in a particular judgment that refers his life to Christ.

Commenting on these two parables, the Pope said that the kingdom of God, though it requires our cooperation, is first of all the gift of the Lord. Our small work, which seems so little before the problems of the world, when placed in God's hands does not fear difficulties: the victory of the Lord is certain.
saints: Today is the feast day of St Antony, so dear to Catholics all over India, but this year it falls on a Sunday and gives way to the Lord's Day. The Tuesday devotions, the novenas of the thirteen Tuesdays and St Antony's bread for the poor may go on as usual, outside the Mass.
14–18 June: weekdays of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time (no memorials in the General Calendar). 19 June: St Romuald, abbot (optional). Next Sunday, 20 June: the Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-13.prayer: Lord God, you take the tender sprig and plant it on the mountain, you bring low the high tree and make the low tree flourish. We thank you for the seed of your word sown in our hearts, and for the growth you give by night and by day, when we do not know how. Lord Jesus, your kingdom is like a mustard seed: make our small faith grow, so that our families and our parish may be a shelter for the poor, the lonely and the stranger. Holy Spirit, keep us green and full of sap even in old age, and help us to walk by faith, not by sight, making it our aim to please you, until we stand before the judgment seat of Christ and are gathered into the harvest of your kingdom. Mary, Mother of the Church, who kept the seed of the Word in your heart, pray for us. Amen.

quick: Ezekiel: God himself will take a tender sprig from the top of the cedar and plant it on a high mountain, where it will become a noble cedar sheltering every kind of bird.
Paul: we walk by faith, not by sight; we make it our aim to please the Lord, for all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
Jesus: the kingdom of God is like seed that grows by itself while the farmer sleeps, and like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, that becomes the greatest of shrubs.
2027-06-13.action: Sow one small seed of faith this week, a kind word, an invitation or a prayer, and leave the growth to God.
2027-06-13.question: Do I trust God with the slow, hidden growth of his kingdom in me and in those I love?
catechism: The Church, seed and beginning of the kingdom.
kidsaint: St Thérèse of Lisieux and the little way

St Thérèse lived in France about a hundred and thirty years ago and died when she was only twenty-four. She never did anything famous. She smiled at a sister who annoyed her, she did small jobs with love, and she offered everything to Jesus. She called this her “little way.” Today she is a Doctor of the Church and patron of the missions! Her small seeds of love grew into a great tree. Lesson: Jesus can make big things grow from the small good things you do every day.
2027-06-13.special: Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year B: Gloria and Creed. St Antony of Padua is omitted because the date falls on a Sunday. Liturgical colour: green.
term: From the Greek parabolē, “a placing side by side.” A parable puts an ordinary thing (a seed, a lamp, a lost coin) beside the mystery of God's kingdom, so that the listener must think, choose and act. Jesus used parables to invite people in, not to give them a lecture.

family.explain: A farmer plants seeds and goes to sleep. He wakes up, he sleeps again, and the seeds grow all by themselves. He does not know how! Jesus says God's kingdom grows like that: quietly, even when we cannot see it. A mustard seed is tiny, smaller than a grain of rice, but it grows into a big plant where birds build their nests. When we do small good things with love, God makes them grow.
family.intention: We pray for farmers who are sowing in the monsoon rains, for children starting a new school year, and for the elderly, that they may stay green and fruitful.
family.ask: Ask: “What small seed of goodness can each of us plant this week?” Then plant a real seed in a pot together and watch it grow.

illus: A retired teacher in a village near Thrissur used to keep a small notebook of the names of her former pupils. Every evening she prayed for five of them. Most of them she never saw again. Years after her death, one of them, now a priest in a mission in Madhya Pradesh, came to the parish to celebrate Mass for her. He told the people that when he was a frightened boy of twelve she had once stayed after class to help him with his lessons, and had said: I will pray for you every week. He had not thought of it for years, but it was that small seed, he said, that God had made grow. The teacher never knew. The seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord, it is good to give thanks to you, to declare your steadfast love in the morning and your faithfulness by night. Sow your word in our hearts and make it grow. Amen.
share: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar (Ezekiel 17:22). Where has God planted something new in my life when everything seemed broken?
The seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how (Mark 4:27). What growth am I impatient for, in myself or in someone I love?
We walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). Where am I being asked to trust what I cannot see?
pm.resp: Lord, it is good to give thanks to you.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a mustard tree in whose shade the nations find a home.
For farmers sowing with the monsoon, and for those whose fields and houses suffer from floods and landslides.
For children and teachers beginning the new school year, that knowledge and faith may grow together in them.
For the elderly, that in old age they may still bear fruit and be honoured among us.
For all who honour St Antony of Padua, that like him they may love the poor and the word of God.
For our group, that we may sow patiently and leave the growth to God.
pm.close: Father, you give the growth to every seed sown in faith. Make your kingdom grow in us, quietly and surely, until the harvest. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, in these weeks of June the monsoon arrives in Kerala, and anyone who has lived in a village knows what happens after the first rains. The dry red earth turns green almost overnight. Seeds that lay hidden in the soil for months suddenly push up their small shoots. Nobody pulled them up; nobody told them to grow. Today's readings are full of this mystery of growth.

In the first reading Ezekiel speaks to a people in exile. Their king has been taken to Babylon, the royal tree of David seems cut down. And God says: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar; I will set it out (Ezekiel 17:22). What the great empires broke, God replants. And the small, tender shoot becomes a noble cedar where every kind of bird finds shelter. God's way is always the same: I bring low the high tree, I make high the low tree (Ezekiel 17:24). It is the song of Mary in the Magnificat: he has brought down the powerful and lifted up the lowly.

In the Gospel Jesus tells of a farmer who scatters seed and then goes to sleep. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how (Mark 4:27). This is a great comfort for parents, teachers, catechists and priests. We sow, and often we see nothing. A child seems to forget everything we taught. A husband does not come back to the sacraments. A parish seems to sleep. Jesus says: do your part, and trust the seed. The power of growth is not in you; it is in the word of God.

Then he speaks of the mustard seed, the smallest of all the seeds on earth (Mark 4:31). The kingdom of God did not begin with armies or palaces. It began in a stable in Bethlehem, in a carpenter's house in Nazareth, with twelve ordinary men. It began, in our own land, with a few families on the coast who received the faith long ago. Today it is a great tree. Never despise small beginnings: a small prayer group, a small act of kindness, a small Sunday school class.

St Paul tells us what kind of life this growth asks of us: we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). We cannot see the growth, but we make it our aim to please him. And Paul reminds us that there will be a harvest: all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). What we sow now, we will reap then.

Today is also the day of St Antony of Padua, though this year the Sunday takes its place. Many of you will go to his shrine or keep his Tuesday devotions. He was a great sower of the word, and he loved the poor. Let us ask his prayers, and let us go home today to sow one small seed: a word of faith, an act of forgiveness, a gift to someone in need. Then let us go to sleep in peace. God will give the growth. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever planted a seed? You put it in the soil, you water it, and then you wait. You cannot see anything happening! But one day a little green shoot comes up. Jesus says God's kingdom is like that. When you pray, when you share, when you say sorry, you are planting little seeds. You cannot see them grow, but God makes them grow.

Jesus also talked about the mustard seed. It is so tiny, smaller than a grain of rice! But it grows into a big plant, and birds come and make their nests in it. So never think: I am too small to do anything for Jesus. Small seeds become big trees. Today, plant one seed of love at home: help your mother, share your toys, or say a prayer for someone who is sad.

intro: Theme: “The seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.”
The cedar God himself replants, the seed that grows by itself, the smallest of all seeds, and the life of faith that waits for the harvest.

q: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar; I will set it out. I will break off a tender one from the topmost of its young twigs; I myself will plant it on a high and lofty mountain.
I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
points.apply: Bring to God in prayer one part of your life that seems broken, and ask him to plant something new there.

q: For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there until they have watered the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty,
The kingdom of God is as if someone would scatter seed on the ground, and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.
points.apply: Keep praying for someone in whom you see no change, and thank God each day for the growth you cannot see.

points.h: The smallest of all the seeds
sub: A garden plant, not a mighty cedar.
q: For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice,

It is like a mustard seed, which, when sown upon the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth; yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes the greatest of all shrubs, and puts forth large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.
points.apply: Do one small thing for the kingdom this week that no one will notice: a visit, a gift, a hidden prayer.

sub: At home in the body, away from the Lord.
The harvest before the judgment seat.
q: The righteous flourish like the palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the Lord; they flourish in the courts of our God. In old age they still produce fruit; they are always green and full of sap,
for we walk by faith, not by sight.
points.apply: Each night this week, before sleeping, ask: what did I sow today that will please the Lord at the harvest?

concl: God plants, the seed grows by his power, and the kingdom begins small but shelters all.
Our part is to sow in faith, to wait in patience and to live so as to please the Lord until the harvest.
2027-06-13.resolve: Sow one seed of faith or kindness each day this week, and leave the growth to God.
